explainers.title: Welcome to your final Year 7 unit
explainers.body:
Welcome to Unit 6 at Ehel Academy. This is the last unit of Year 7, and it teaches the sixth and final Global Perspectives skill: Communication. You have travelled a long way this year, and this unit is where all of that work finally reaches other people.

Remember the six skills you have been building:

Communication is placed last for a good reason. It is the skill that brings all the others together. You can research a topic brilliantly, analyse it deeply and evaluate it fairly, but if you cannot share what you have learned, it stays locked inside your own head. Communication is how your thinking becomes something a listener can hear, a reader can follow, and a community can act on.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in Ehel Academy's self-paced way, which means three kinds of support work together:

In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'present to the class' or 'share with your group'. In our model, your presentation has two stages. First you rehearse with your AI tutor, who acts as a patient, honest audience and helps you improve. Then you deliver the real thing in your teacher session, and often to your family at home. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it as a rehearsal in front of a real listener. Say your ideas out loud, and let the tutor tell you what came across clearly and what did not.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down to rehearse a tricky sentence, or move quickly through an idea you already know.

Your AI tutor, available 24 hours a day. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were both a practice audience and a helpful coach in one. It will listen to your ideas, ask you questions, and give you feedback at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. Your live sessions are where you deliver your real presentation, hear other learners, and get to know your class.

explainers.title: Meet Arjun, our communicator for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 7 learner all the way through the unit. His name is Arjun, and he is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

All year, Arjun has been working on one Challenge: the busy road just outside the school gate. He noticed that crossing it at home time felt dangerous, with cars and minibuses moving fast while crowds of students waited to cross. Over the year he has researched the problem with a survey and by observing the junction, analysed what causes the danger and what it leads to, and evaluated several possible solutions to see which would work best.

Now Arjun reaches the final step. He has strong findings, but they are still sitting in his notebook. In this unit he must communicate them: turn them into a clear, convincing presentation that his teacher, his family and even the local community could understand and act on. As you meet each new skill, you will see exactly what Arjun does with it. You will be doing the very same thing with your own Challenge.

explainers.title: Your Challenge comes together and is shared
explainers.body:
All year, your work has been building towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge: a global topic that also matters right where you live. In each unit you added another skill to it. Communication is the unit where the Challenge finally comes together and is shared with an audience.

Think of your Challenge as a house you have been building all year. Research laid the foundations. Analysis and Evaluation raised the walls and checked they were strong. Communication is the moment you open the door and invite people inside. Everything you present in this unit rests on the work you already did.

explainers.title: What is communication, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think communication just means talking. In Global Perspectives it means something more careful. Communication is transferring information from one person to another, by speaking or writing, in a way that the other person truly understands. The test of good communication is not whether you spoke, but whether your listener understood.

Communication has two halves that matter equally:

Weak communicators only think about the first half. Strong communicators do both: they make themselves clear, and they listen closely to others. You will practise both halves in this unit.
bullets: Expressing — getting your own ideas out clearly, whether by speaking, writing, or showing a visual.
Listening — taking in other people's ideas carefully, so you understand them and can respond well.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Knowing your purpose and audience
explainers.body:
Before you plan a single sentence, a strong communicator asks two questions: What is my purpose? and Who is my audience? These two answers shape everything else.

The same message must be shaped differently for different audiences. If you were explaining road safety to a class of six-year-olds, you would use simple words and a friendly voice. If you were writing to the town council, you would be more formal and lead with your strongest evidence. Same topic, different shape, because the audience is different.
bullets: Purpose is why you are communicating. Do you want to inform people, persuade them, or simply raise awareness? Your purpose decides what you include.
Audience is who you are communicating with. Their age, their knowledge and their interests decide how you say it.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Finding the key message
explainers.body:
Every good piece of communication has one key message: the single most important idea you want your audience to remember. If your listener forgot everything else but remembered your key message, you would still have succeeded. Weak communication has no clear message, so the audience is left wondering what the point was.

You need this skill in two ways. First, when you read or listen to something, you should be able to find its key message. Second, when you create something, you should be able to say your own key message in one sentence.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Structuring your piece - introduction, body and conclusion
explainers.body:
A clear message needs a clear structure. Structure is simply how your piece is organised so that the audience can follow it. Almost every good talk, essay or article is built from three parts:

Each part has a job. The introduction makes it clear what you are talking about, so no one is lost. The body does the real work: each paragraph or point should carry one main idea and the evidence that backs it up. The conclusion reminds the audience of your message and leaves them with a strong final thought. A common mistake is to sneak a brand-new idea into the conclusion. Do not: a conclusion only sums up what you already said.
bullets: Introduction — tells the audience what your piece is about and states your key message.
Body — the middle, usually several paragraphs or points, where you explain your ideas and give your evidence.
Conclusion — draws your points together and sums up, without adding anything new.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Building a structured argument with evidence
explainers.body:
Often your purpose is to persuade, and that means building an argument. In Global Perspectives, an argument is not a quarrel. It is a claim backed up by good thinking. A strong argument has three parts:

This is exactly where your earlier skills pay off. Your evidence comes from your Research. Your reasons often come from your Analysis of causes and effects. Your judgement about which solution is best comes from your Evaluation. Communication does not invent new material; it arranges the material you already earned into a convincing shape.
bullets: A claim — what you want your audience to accept, such as 'the road should be made safer'.
Reasons — why the claim is true, such as 'because students cannot cross safely'.
Evidence — the facts that support each reason, such as survey results or an observation.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Giving reasons and linking your ideas
explainers.body:
Good communication does not just list facts; it connects them so the audience can follow your thinking. You do this with small linking words, sometimes called transition words. They act like signposts that tell your audience what is coming next.

Two kinds are especially useful:

There are also linking words for finishing, such as 'finally', 'to sum up', 'in conclusion' and 'as you can see'. These signal that you are drawing everything together. Used well, linking words turn a pile of separate facts into a smooth, reasoned argument.
bullets: Words that give a reason — such as 'because', 'so that', 'due to' and 'this means that'. They show why something matters.
Words that introduce evidence — such as 'for example', 'for instance', 'such as' and 'to show this'. They tell the audience a fact is coming.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Presenting your ideas out loud
explainers.body:
When you present orally, how you speak matters almost as much as what you say. The good news is that clear speaking is a set of habits anyone can learn, not a magic gift. Keep these in mind:

The single best way to get better at speaking is to rehearse out loud before the real thing. Reading your talk silently is not the same. This is where your AI tutor is perfect: you can present to it again and again, at any hour, and it will tell you honestly whether you were clear.
bullets: Speak slowly and clearly. Nervous speakers rush. Slow down, and give your audience time to take each idea in.
Give details, but stay on your point. Enough detail to be convincing, not so much that your message is buried.
Use notes, not a script. A few bullet points on a card keep you on track without you reading every word.
Look up. Making eye contact, even now and then, shows the audience you are talking to them.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Presenting your ideas visually
explainers.body:
Not all communication is spoken. Often a visual — a poster, a chart, a diagram or a slogan — carries your message faster than words alone. A good visual is not decoration; it helps the audience understand something more quickly.

Two visual tools are especially useful in Global Perspectives:
bullets: Simple charts — a bar chart or table can show a number pattern in a second, far faster than a sentence. If your evidence is numbers, a chart is often the clearest choice.
Slogans — a short, memorable phrase that raises awareness of an issue. Slogans work because they are short, so people remember them.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Choosing suitable language and register
explainers.body:
Register means the level of formality in your language, and choosing the right one for your audience. You already do this without thinking: you speak to a young child differently from the way you speak to a head teacher. Matching your register to your audience is a real communication skill.

Getting register wrong sends the wrong signal. Language that is too casual for the town council may seem as if you are not taking the issue seriously. Language that is too formal for young children will simply lose them. The trick is to picture your audience and ask: what kind of language would they take seriously and understand?
bullets: Formal register — careful, polite, no slang. Suits a letter to officials, or a serious presentation.
Friendly register — warm and simple, still respectful. Suits younger audiences, family, or awareness posters.

explainers.title: Skill 9: Listening actively and giving helpful feedback
explainers.body:
Communication is a two-way street, so listening is half the skill. Active listening means attentively trying to understand what someone means, rather than just hearing their words while you wait for your turn to speak. It is one of the most respectful things you can do for another person.

You show active listening with feedback of two kinds:

Active listening also helps you give better feedback on other people's work, which you will do in your teacher sessions. Good feedback follows three fair rules: start with something positive, give more positives than negatives, and always talk about the work, not the person. 'Your evidence in the second point was very convincing' helps someone improve. 'You are a bad speaker' only hurts.
bullets: Non-verbal feedback — showing you are listening without words: nodding, leaning forward, and making eye contact.
Verbal feedback — short spoken signals such as 'I see', 'I understand' and 'that makes sense'.

explainers.title: Skill 10: Communicating fairly and referencing sources
explainers.body:
Global Perspectives is about seeing an issue from many sides. So when you communicate, you should represent different perspectives fairly, not just your own. An audience trusts a communicator who has clearly listened to more than one point of view, and who gives credit for the evidence they use.

Two habits make your communication fair and trustworthy:
bullets: Represent other perspectives. Mention the views of people who see the issue differently, and treat them fairly, even as you argue your own case.
Reference your sources. When your evidence comes from a book, website, report or person, say so. This is honest, it avoids copying, and it lets your audience check your facts.

explainers.title: Skill 11: Reflecting on how your audience responded
explainers.body:
The last part of communication happens after you present. A thoughtful communicator watches and listens to how the audience responded, then uses what they notice to improve next time. This is where Communication joins hands with Reflection, the skill you built earlier in the year.

After you present, ask yourself:

Audience reactions are information, not judgement. A confused look is not a failure; it is a clue that points you to the sentence you need to fix. Every presentation you give makes the next one stronger, as long as you reflect on it honestly.
bullets: Did my audience understand my key message? How could I tell?
Which part landed well, and which part left them confused or bored?
What questions did they ask, and what do those questions tell me was unclear?
What one thing would I change next time?

explainers.title: How Communication draws on all five earlier skills
explainers.body:
Communication is placed last because it needs the other five. A brilliant presentation is really the other skills, made visible to an audience. Look at how each one feeds in:

So when you communicate your Challenge, you are not starting from nothing. You are gathering everything you built all year and presenting it as one clear, convincing whole. That is why this skill comes last: it is the destination the other five were leading to.
bullets: Research gives you the facts and sources that become your evidence. Without research, you would have nothing true to say.
Analysis gives you the reasons: the causes and effects you found when you broke the topic apart.
Evaluation gives you your judgement: which solution is strongest, and why your audience should accept it.
Reflection helps you improve, as you notice how your audience responded and change your message.
Collaboration helps you listen and give feedback well, so that presenting and discussing with others goes smoothly.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: Arjun's Challenge, communicated
explainers.body: You have now met every communication skill in this unit. Here is how Arjun used them to turn a year of work into one clear presentation:

explainers.title: You have completed the Year 7 skills journey
explainers.body:
Take a moment to see how far you have come. At the start of the year you met Research, and learned to find things out carefully. Then Analysis taught you to break a topic apart, Evaluation taught you to judge how strong ideas really are, Reflection taught you to learn from your own thinking, and Collaboration taught you to work well with others. Now Communication has taught you to share it all clearly with the world.

These six skills are not just for Global Perspectives. They are for the rest of your life: for the choices you will make, the problems you will help solve, and the ideas you will one day need to explain to others. A person who can research, analyse, evaluate, reflect, collaborate and communicate can take on almost anything.

Well done for reaching the end of Year 7. Finish this unit by communicating your Challenge as clearly and fairly as you can, and be proud of the thinker you have become. In the Activities file, your final presentation is waiting.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: Communication is not just talking. It is making sure another person truly understands you.
It works in two directions: getting your own message across clearly, and listening carefully to others.
In this unit, everything you researched, analysed and evaluated across Year 7 turns into a clear message you can present.

bigIdeas.title: Who is your audience in this unit?
lines: Your AI tutor is your rehearsal audience. Practise with it as often as you like, at any hour, until your message is clear.
Your teacher session, about twice a week, is where you deliver the real presentation to your teacher and other learners.
Your family and community are a real audience too. Sharing your Challenge at home is one of the most powerful things you can do.

You do not have to make it perfect on the first try. Communication improves with rehearsal, exactly like a sport or a song. That is why your AI tutor matters so much: it will listen as many times as you need, without ever getting tired.

bigIdeas.title: A trick for finding a key message
lines: Look for words or ideas that are repeated. Writers and speakers repeat what matters most.
Ask: what is the one thing this person most wants me to remember?
Try to say it in a single sentence. If you cannot, keep trimming until you can.

The same trick works on your own Challenge. Before you plan your presentation, force yourself to write your key message as one clear sentence. If you cannot say it in a sentence, you are not ready to present yet.

bigIdeas.title: Claim, reason, evidence - the backbone of persuasion
lines: Claim: what you believe should happen.
Reason: why you believe it.
Evidence: the fact, number or example that proves the reason.
A claim with no evidence is only an opinion. Evidence is what makes an audience believe you.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a strong slogan
lines: Keep it short. Short sentences are easy to remember.
Make the point clear at a glance, with no confusing words.
Where you can, give a reason or a feeling, so it sticks in the mind.
Example shape: a strong phrase, then a reason — Slow down, save a life.

bigIdeas.title: Fair feedback in one line
lines: Start with a genuine positive.
Give more positives than negatives.
Talk about the work, not the person, and offer one clear idea to improve.

bigIdeas.title: A fairness note for Global Perspectives
lines: A fair communicator can present an issue that different families feel differently about, such as whether a school calendar should include holidays for both Eid and Christmas, by giving each viewpoint honestly.
You can still have your own opinion. Fairness means you form it after listening to all sides, and you let the audience hear those sides too.
Representing perspectives evenly, without putting one group down, is at the heart of good communication.

bigIdeas.title: Where this unit is heading
lines: By the end of these activities you will have a finished presentation about your Challenge.
You will rehearse it fully with your AI tutor, then deliver it in your teacher session and, if you can, to your family.
You will also design a visual, such as a poster with a slogan, to share your message quickly.

bigIdeas.title: A quick structure check
lines: Introduction: does it make clear what I am talking about and what I believe?
Body: does each point carry just one main idea?
Conclusion: does it only sum up, with nothing new sneaking in?

bigIdeas.title: Handy linking words
lines: To give a reason: because, so that, due to, this means that.
To introduce evidence: for example, for instance, such as, to show this.
To conclude: finally, in conclusion, to sum up, as you can see.

bigIdeas.title: Rehearsal tips
lines: Speak slowly and clearly, and pause after your key message.
Use a few bullet-point notes, not a full script you read word for word.
Rehearse as many times as you like — your AI tutor never gets tired.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 6 of Global Perspectives, the final unit of Year 7, and the skill is Communication.
Ask it: In one or two sentences, why is communication a useful skill even outside of school?
Then tell the tutor which part of communicating worries you most — speaking out loud, organising your ideas, or something else — and ask for one tip to start with.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think communication means.
Ask it: Is my definition missing anything important, such as listening?
Then try Arjun's test: explain your Challenge topic to your tutor in thirty seconds, and ask whether your main message came across clearly.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your Challenge topic and what you want your audience to think, feel or do by the end.
Ask it to help you name your purpose in one word: inform, persuade, or raise awareness.
Then describe your main audience, and ask the tutor how that audience should change the way you speak or write.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your AI tutor a short passage or ask it to give you one, then tell the tutor what you think the key message is.
Ask it whether you found the true main idea, and how it spotted the message.
Then say your own Challenge key message in one sentence, and ask the tutor if it is clear and focused enough.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the topic of your presentation.
Ask it to help you draft a one-sentence introduction, three body points, and a conclusion that adds nothing new.
Then check together: does each body point carry just one main idea?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one claim you want to make about your Challenge.
Ask it to help you add a reason and a piece of real evidence from your own research, analysis or evaluation.
Then ask: where did this evidence come from, and how should I mention that source when I present?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your AI tutor two or three facts from your Challenge with no linking words between them.
Ask it to help you join them using words like because, so that, and for example.
Then ask the tutor which linking words would suit the conclusion of your presentation.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your introduction and first body point out loud to your AI tutor, as if it were your audience.
Ask it: Was I clear? Did I go too fast? Was my key message easy to hear?
Ask the tutor for one specific thing to improve, then present again and see if it is better.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what evidence you have and who your visual is for.
Ask it whether a chart, a diagram or a slogan would show your message most clearly.
Then draft a slogan for your Challenge and ask the tutor if it is short, clear and memorable.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor who your main audience is for your Challenge presentation.
Ask it whether a formal or a friendly register would suit them better, and why.
Then say one sentence of your talk, and ask the tutor to rewrite it in the register that fits your audience.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to read you a short opinion on a topic, then tell it the key message back in your own words to show you listened.
Ask it to explain the difference between verbal and non-verbal feedback with an example of each.
Then present a piece of your own work and ask the tutor to give you feedback using the three fair rules.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your main argument, then ask it to help you name one perspective that differs from yours.
Ask how you could mention that other view fairly without weakening your own case.
Then list the sources of your evidence and ask the tutor how to reference them simply when you speak.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: After you rehearse, tell your AI tutor which part of your presentation you think was clearest and which was weakest.
Ask it to predict what questions a real audience might ask, so you can prepare answers.
Then ask the tutor to help you plan one improvement for your next rehearsal.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic, your purpose and your audience.
Ask it: Does my purpose match my audience, or should I adjust one of them?
Ask the tutor how my chosen audience should change the way I speak or write.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your key message to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Is this clear and focused, or is it trying to say too much at once?
Ask the tutor to suggest one sharper way to word my key message.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your introduction, three body points and conclusion to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the structure is clear and whether any point is doing two jobs at once.
Ask the tutor if my conclusion accidentally introduces a new idea.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your three body points and the evidence you have for each.
Ask it: Which point has the strongest evidence, and which is the weakest?
Ask the tutor how to mention the source of each piece of evidence when I present.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read one of your points to your AI tutor as a claim, a reason and evidence.
Ask it: Does my reason really explain my claim, and does my evidence really prove my reason?
Ask the tutor to help me strengthen the weakest of my three arguments.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your linked-up argument to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the linking words make your reasoning clearer, or whether any feel forced.
Ask the tutor to suggest one more linking word that would help my flow.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your visual and read your slogan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the visual shows your evidence clearly and whether the slogan is memorable.
Ask the tutor for one way to make my slogan shorter or stronger.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two versions — friendly and formal — to your AI tutor.
Ask it which register best fits my real audience, and why.
Ask the tutor to check that my presentation keeps that register from start to finish.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your full talk to your AI tutor and ask for honest feedback on clarity and pace.
Ask it to predict two questions a real audience might ask, and help me prepare answers.
Ask the tutor: what is the single most important thing to improve before my teacher session?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor how your real presentation went and what questions people asked.
Ask it to help me understand what those questions show about the clearest and weakest parts of my talk.
Ask the tutor to help me plan one improvement for the next time I present.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three checkpoint sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Based on how my audience responded, what is one communication skill I should keep practising?
Ask the tutor to help me set one goal for communicating in Year 8.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fixed pieces and your rewritten feedback to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your rewrites are now clear, well structured and fair.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to improve any answer you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was strongest and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking and your confidence changed across the whole year.
Ask the tutor to suggest one skill to focus on first in Year 8, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's starting point
lines: Arjun knows a lot about the road outside school. But when he first tried to explain it to his uncle, he jumped around: a bit about cars, a bit about his survey, a bit about a fence, all mixed up.
His uncle was kind but confused, and asked: So what are you actually saying?
Arjun realised the problem was not his research. It was his communication. His message was strong but unclear.
This unit is about fixing exactly that: turning good thinking into a clear message an audience can follow.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's example: purpose and audience
lines: Purpose: Arjun wants to persuade people that the road outside Ehel Academy should be made safer.
Audience 1: his teacher session and family. He will use a clear spoken presentation with a friendly, respectful voice.
Audience 2: the local community. For them he plans a poster with a short slogan, because a poster is seen quickly by many people.
Notice that Arjun keeps one message but changes its shape for each audience.

speakingPrompts.title: Nadia's example: finding the message in a text
lines: Nadia reads a short article that repeats the words hand-washing, illness and clean water.
She asks herself: if I had to sum this whole text up in one sentence, what would it be?
Her answer: washing hands with clean water stops many illnesses from spreading.
That one sentence is the key message. Everything else in the article is a detail that supports it.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's example: the shape of his talk
lines: Introduction: The road outside our school is dangerous at home time, and I will show why it should be made safer.
Body point 1: My survey found that most students feel unsafe crossing.
Body point 2: I observed cars moving fast while crowds waited, which explains why.
Body point 3: Of the solutions I evaluated, a proper crossing would help the most.
Conclusion: For all these reasons, our town should add a safe crossing outside Ehel Academy. No new facts, just a strong finish.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's example: one body point as an argument
lines: Claim: The road outside our school should have a safe crossing.
Reason: Because students have to cross through fast-moving traffic with no safe place to do it.
Evidence: In my survey, 17 of 24 students said they feel unsafe crossing at home time, and when I observed the road, cars did not slow down for the crowd.
The reason explains the claim, and the evidence proves the reason. That is a complete little argument.

Notice that Arjun references his evidence: he says it came from his own survey and observation. When your evidence comes from a book, a website or a report, you should name that source too, just as you learned in Research. Naming your sources is honest, and it makes your audience trust you more.

speakingPrompts.title: Zara's example: adding linking words
lines: Without links: The market floods. There are plastic bags in the drains. We should use cloth bags.
With links: The market floods because plastic bags block the drains. This means that switching to cloth bags would help. For example, one nearby town cut its flooding after banning thin bags.
The second version reasons; the first only lists. The linking words do the work.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's example: rehearsing with his AI tutor
lines: Arjun read his talk in his head and thought it was fine.
Then he said it out loud to his AI tutor, who noticed he spoke very fast and never paused.
On his third rehearsal he slowed down, paused after his key message, and it sounded far more convincing.
By the time of his teacher session, he had practised so often that his nerves had mostly gone.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's example: a poster and a slogan
lines: For his community audience, Arjun designs a poster showing a simple bar chart of his survey: most students feel unsafe crossing.
Across the top he writes a short slogan: Cross in safety — slow the traffic outside our school.
The chart gives the evidence at a glance; the slogan gives the message in a few words.
A busy passer-by understands his point in seconds, which a long paragraph could never do.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's example: two registers, one message
lines: To six-year-olds: The road is busy, so we must always hold a grown-up's hand and cross carefully.
To the town council: The current crossing arrangements place students at risk, and I respectfully ask the council to consider a safe crossing point.
Same concern, two registers. Each fits its audience.

speakingPrompts.title: Leila's example: feedback that helps
lines: Leila listens to Arjun rehearse and gives feedback.
She starts positive: Your survey evidence was really convincing.
She adds one improvement about the work: I lost your key message at the start — could you say it more slowly?
That is kind, specific, and about the work, so Arjun knows exactly what to fix.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's example: fairness and credit
lines: Arjun argues for a safe crossing, but he also fairly mentions the shopkeepers who worry that speed bumps could slow deliveries.
By naming that other perspective honestly, he sounds fair, not one-sided.
He also says where his facts came from: my own survey of 24 students, and a road-safety leaflet from a named charity.
His audience trusts him more because he is fair and open about his evidence.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's example: learning from the response
lines: After his teacher session, Arjun noticed two people asked the same question: how much would a crossing cost?
That told him his talk had a gap: he had no evidence about cost.
Instead of feeling bad, he added a cost point to his poster for the community.
The audience's questions made his communication better.

speakingPrompts.title: Arjun's whole journey, from notebook to audience
lines: Skill 1: He named his purpose (to persuade) and his audiences (teacher session, family, community).
Skills 2 and 3: He wrote his key message in one sentence and shaped his talk into introduction, body and conclusion.
Skills 4 and 5: He built each body point as a claim with a reason and evidence, joined by linking words.
Skills 6 and 7: He rehearsed out loud with his AI tutor and designed a poster with a chart and a slogan.
Skill 8: He matched his register to each audience, formal for the council and friendly for children.
Skills 9 and 10: He listened to feedback, represented other perspectives fairly, and referenced his sources.
Skill 11: He reflected on the questions people asked and improved his message for next time.

By following these steps, Arjun turned a worry about a dangerous road into a clear, fair, evidence-backed presentation that his community could act on. In the Activities file, you will do exactly the same with your own Challenge, one step at a time, rehearsing with your AI tutor and delivering in your teacher session.

speakingPrompts.title: Karim's example: purpose and audience
lines: Topic: plastic waste washing up on the Berbera coast.
Purpose: to raise awareness, so more people take their rubbish home.
Audience: families who visit the beach at the weekend.
What he wants: for visitors to notice the problem and carry a bag for their litter.

speakingPrompts.title: A model key message
lines: Weak: There are lots of things about the road and traffic and students and safety near our school.
Strong: The road outside our school should be made safer with a proper crossing.
The strong version is one clear sentence that an audience can hold in their head.

speakingPrompts.title: Leila's example: gathering evidence for one point
lines: Leila's Challenge is about traffic near her school in Mogadishu.
From her research: 15 of 20 drivers she counted did not slow down at the corner.
From her analysis: fast traffic plus a blind corner is what makes it dangerous.
From her evaluation: she judged that a painted crossing was the cheapest useful fix.
She now has a number, a cause, and a judgement — a full point ready to present.

speakingPrompts.title: A model point built as an argument
lines: Claim: Our market should switch to reusable cloth bags.
Reason: Because thin plastic bags block the drains and cause flooding.
Evidence: In my survey, most sellers agreed the drains flood in the rains.
Source: my own survey of 20 market sellers.

speakingPrompts.title: Model slogans
lines: Water: Every drop counts — do not waste water.
Road safety: Slow down outside our school — keep students safe.
Plastic: Say no to thin bags — bring your own.
Notice each one is short, clear, and gives a reason or a feeling.

A visual is not decoration; it should make one idea easier to grasp. If a passer-by cannot understand your poster in a few seconds, it is trying to say too much. Cut words until only your key message and your strongest piece of evidence remain. A single clear number, a simple drawing, and a short slogan will beat a crowded page every time.

speakingPrompts.title: Yasmin's example: one message, two registers
lines: Message: girls who leave school early lose chances they cannot easily get back.
Friendly (for younger students): staying in school opens doors that are hard to open later.
Formal (for a community meeting): early school-leaving among girls reduces their future opportunities, and I ask you to consider how we might support them to stay.
Same message, matched to each audience.

speakingPrompts.title: Share it at home too
lines: Present your Challenge to a family member or neighbour, in a register that suits them.
Ask them what they think should be done about your topic.
Bring their response, and any questions they asked, to your next teacher session.

toolkit.title: The communication cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro:
Whatever your message, good communication follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel unsure.

The steps run in order, but you can always loop back. If your rehearsal shows your message is unclear, return to the key-message step and sharpen it. If a point has no evidence, return to your Year 7 research. Good communicators move around this cycle more than once before they present.
items: Purpose and audience: decide why you are communicating and who for.
Key message: say your one main idea in a single sentence.
Structure: organise it into an introduction, a body, and a conclusion.
Evidence: support each point with a fact, and name its source.
Rehearse: practise out loud with your AI tutor and improve.
Deliver: present in your teacher session, and to family and community.
Reflect: notice how your audience responded, and improve for next time.

toolkit.title: The Communication skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Communication is transferring information from one person to another, by speaking or writing, in a way that the other person truly understands. It is not just talking. Real communication means knowing your purpose and audience, organising a clear message with evidence, presenting it well by voice or visual, and listening carefully to others.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always think about your audience, because a message only works if the person in front of you understands it. Second, remember communication is two-way: you must listen as carefully as you speak. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 7 Communication objectives
toolkit.intro:
Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong communication looks like at this stage. There are two Communication objectives, restated simply below. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

Notice that these two objectives cover the two halves of communication. Objective 6.1 is about expressing your own ideas well: clearly, with reasons, and with sources named. Objective 6.2 is about listening well: taking in what others say and responding in a way that shows you understood. A strong communicator works on both, so aim to grow the two together rather than only the speaking half.

rows: Present information and arguments clearly with some reasoning, referencing sources where appropriate.
Share your ideas and arguments clearly, give reasons, and say where your evidence came from.
Listen to ideas and information and offer relevant and well-judged contributions that demonstrate understanding of the issue.
Listen carefully to others, then add helpful, sensible comments that show you understood the issue.

toolkit.title: Planner: Audience and purpose
toolkit.intro:
Fill this in before you plan anything. Copy the table into your notebook and answer each question.

The most common mistake is to skip this planner and jump straight to writing. Five minutes spent answering these questions will save you an hour of confusion later, because every other choice you make depends on knowing your audience and your purpose.

rows: Who is my audience?
What do they already know about my topic?
What is my purpose: inform, persuade, or raise awareness?
What is my one key message?
Which form fits best: a talk, a poster, a chart, a slogan?
What language and register will suit this audience?

toolkit.title: Template: Introduction, body and conclusion
toolkit.intro:
Use this outline to shape any presentation or piece of writing. Each body point should carry one idea and its evidence.

Three body points is a good number for a Year 7 presentation: enough to be convincing, not so many that your audience loses track. If you have more, choose your three strongest and let the rest go. A short, clear talk beats a long, crowded one every time.

rows: Introduction
Say what the piece is about and state your key message.
Body point 1
First point, with a reason and evidence (and its source).
Body point 2
Second point, with a reason and evidence (and its source).
Body point 3
Third point, with a reason and evidence (and its source).
Conclusion
Sum up your points. Add nothing new.

toolkit.title: Template: Building an argument
toolkit.intro:
Turn any point into a convincing argument by filling in these four rows.

Repeat this pattern for each of your body points. Three short arguments, each with a claim, a reason and evidence, make a far more convincing presentation than a long list of facts with no shape.

rows: Claim
What I want my audience to accept.
Reason
Why the claim is true (often starts with 'because').
Evidence
The fact, number or example that proves the reason.
Source
Where the evidence came from.

toolkit.title: Referencing your evidence when you speak
toolkit.intro:
Objective 6.1 asks you to reference sources 'where appropriate'. You do not need a full written reference list for a short spoken talk, but you should still say where your evidence came from, in a natural sentence. This is honest, it avoids copying, and it makes your audience trust you more.

Simple ways to reference out loud:

If your piece is written rather than spoken, add a short reference list at the end, giving the author, title, date and where you found each source, just as you learned in Research.
items: In my own survey of ... people, I found that ...
According to a report by ... , ...
As one shopkeeper I interviewed told me, ...
A leaflet from ... (name the organisation) says that ...

toolkit.title: Visual-aid tips
toolkit.intro: A good visual makes your message faster to understand, not just prettier. Keep these in mind.
items: Use a chart when your evidence is numbers — it shows a pattern at a glance.
Use a diagram to show how something works or how parts connect.
Keep posters simple: few words, large enough to read from a distance.
Add a slogan: short, clear, and memorable, giving a reason or a feeling.
Make sure every visual actually supports your key message, and remove anything that distracts.

toolkit.title: Register guide
toolkit.intro: Register is your level of formality. Match it to your audience.

rows: Young children
Simple, warm, friendly words; short sentences.
The road is busy, so we always cross with a grown-up.
Family and community
Clear and friendly, still respectful.
Our school road is dangerous at home time, and here is how we can help.
Officials, such as a council
Formal, polite, evidence-first.
I respectfully ask the council to consider a safe crossing outside the school.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for communicating
toolkit.intro: Use these to speak and write clearly. They work for talks, posters and written arguments.

toolkit.title: To introduce your piece
items: Today I will explain / show / argue that ...
This presentation is about ...
My main message is that ...

toolkit.title: To give a reason or introduce evidence
items: This matters because ...
For example, ... / For instance, ...
According to ... (source), ...
My survey / research found that ...

toolkit.title: To conclude
items: To sum up, ...
In conclusion, ...
As you can see, ...
For all these reasons, I believe that ...

toolkit.title: To listen actively and give feedback
items: I see. / I understand. / That makes sense.
So your main point is ...? (checking you understood)
One thing I really liked was ...
One idea to make it even better would be ...

checklists.title: Checklist: Before you present
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, rehearse again.
items: Clear message — I can say my key message in one sentence.
Structure — I have an introduction, a body and a conclusion.
Evidence — every point has a fact, and I can name its source.
Reasoning — I use linking words like 'because' and 'for example'.
Voice — I will speak slowly and clearly, and pause after my message.
Register — my language suits my audience.
Fairness — I mention other perspectives honestly.
Rehearsed — I have practised the whole thing out loud at least twice.

challenge.intro:
You have now communicated a whole year's work. Pull it together by completing these three sentences about your Challenge, in your own words:

Keep this checkpoint safe. It is the final piece of your Year 7 journey, and it shows how much your communication has grown since the very first unit. Notice how much more confident you are now at turning your ideas into a clear message for a real audience.
checkpoints: The clearest part of my message was ...
The part my audience understood least was ...
If I presented this again, I would ...

activities.title: Decide your purpose and audience
activities.label: Activity 1: Decide your purpose and audience
activities.intro: Every strong piece of communication starts here. Before you plan anything, get clear on why you are communicating and who you are communicating with.
steps: Write your Challenge topic in one sentence: 'My Challenge is about ...'.
Name your purpose in one word: to inform, to persuade, or to raise awareness.
Describe your main audience (for example: my teacher session, my family, or the local community).
Write one sentence about what you want that audience to think, feel, or do by the end.

boxes.title: Karim's example: purpose and audience
lines: Topic: plastic waste washing up on the Berbera coast.
Purpose: to raise awareness, so more people take their rubbish home.
Audience: families who visit the beach at the weekend.
What he wants: for visitors to notice the problem and carry a bag for their litter.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic, your purpose and your audience.
Ask it: Does my purpose match my audience, or should I adjust one of them?
Ask the tutor how my chosen audience should change the way I speak or write.

activities.title: Write your key message
activities.label: Activity 2: Write your key message
activities.intro: Your key message is the one idea you most want your audience to remember. Everything else in your presentation will support it, so it is worth getting right.
steps: Look back over your Challenge work from the year: your research, your analysis, your evaluation.
Ask yourself: if my audience forgot everything but one sentence, what should it be?
Write your key message as a single, clear sentence.
Read it aloud. If it takes more than one breath or needs a second sentence, trim it.

boxes.title: A model key message
lines: Weak: There are lots of things about the road and traffic and students and safety near our school.
Strong: The road outside our school should be made safer with a proper crossing.
The strong version is one clear sentence that an audience can hold in their head.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your key message to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Is this clear and focused, or is it trying to say too much at once?
Ask the tutor to suggest one sharper way to word my key message.

activities.title: Plan your structure - introduction, body, conclusion
activities.label: Activity 3: Plan your structure - introduction, body, conclusion
activities.intro: Now give your presentation a clear shape. Use the three-part structure: an introduction that states your message, a body that carries your points and evidence, and a conclusion that sums up without adding anything new.
steps: Introduction: write one or two sentences that say what your presentation is about and state your key message.
Body: plan three points. For each, write the point in a few words. You will add evidence in the next activity.
Conclusion: write one or two sentences that draw your points together. Do not add any new fact here.
Read the whole plan through. Does each part do its job?

boxes.title: A quick structure check
lines: Introduction: does it make clear what I am talking about and what I believe?
Body: does each point carry just one main idea?
Conclusion: does it only sum up, with nothing new sneaking in?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your introduction, three body points and conclusion to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the structure is clear and whether any point is doing two jobs at once.
Ask the tutor if my conclusion accidentally introduces a new idea.

activities.title: Gather your evidence from the whole year
activities.label: Activity 4: Gather your evidence from the whole year
activities.intro:
This is the activity where your Challenge truly comes together. Communication does not invent facts; it arranges the ones you already earned. Go back through your Year 7 work and pull out your best material.

Now match your evidence to your three body points from Activity 3. Each point should have at least one piece of real evidence sitting under it. If a point has no evidence, either find some or drop the point. Aim for a mix: a number from a survey is convincing, but so is a short quotation from a person you interviewed, or a fact from a trusted report.
steps: From your Research: find two or three facts, numbers or quotations you can use as evidence.
From your Analysis: find one cause-and-effect idea that explains why your topic matters.
From your Evaluation: find your judgement about which solution or answer is strongest.
Next to each piece of evidence, note where it came from, so you can reference it.

boxes.title: Leila's example: gathering evidence for one point
lines: Leila's Challenge is about traffic near her school in Mogadishu.
From her research: 15 of 20 drivers she counted did not slow down at the corner.
From her analysis: fast traffic plus a blind corner is what makes it dangerous.
From her evaluation: she judged that a painted crossing was the cheapest useful fix.
She now has a number, a cause, and a judgement — a full point ready to present.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your three body points and the evidence you have for each.
Ask it: Which point has the strongest evidence, and which is the weakest?
Ask the tutor how to mention the source of each piece of evidence when I present.

activities.title: Build each point into a structured argument
activities.label: Activity 5: Build each point into a structured argument
activities.intro: Turn each body point into a small argument: a claim, a reason, and evidence. This is what makes a presentation convincing rather than just a list of facts.
steps: For each body point, write the claim (what you want the audience to accept).
Add the reason (why the claim is true), often starting with the word 'because'.
Add the evidence (the fact, number or example that proves the reason).
Name the source of that evidence in a few words.

boxes.title: A model point built as an argument
lines: Claim: Our market should switch to reusable cloth bags.
Reason: Because thin plastic bags block the drains and cause flooding.
Evidence: In my survey, most sellers agreed the drains flood in the rains.
Source: my own survey of 20 market sellers.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read one of your points to your AI tutor as a claim, a reason and evidence.
Ask it: Does my reason really explain my claim, and does my evidence really prove my reason?
Ask the tutor to help me strengthen the weakest of my three arguments.

activities.title: Add reasoning and linking words
activities.label: Activity 6: Add reasoning and linking words
activities.intro: Now join your ideas so your audience can follow your thinking. Linking words are the signposts that turn separate facts into a smooth argument.
steps: Read your three arguments aloud. Where do the ideas feel jumpy or disconnected?
Add reason words such as 'because', 'so that', 'due to' and 'this means that'.
Add evidence words such as 'for example', 'for instance' and 'such as' before each piece of evidence.
Choose a linking phrase for your conclusion, such as 'to sum up', 'finally' or 'as you can see'.

boxes.title: Handy linking words
lines: To give a reason: because, so that, due to, this means that.
To introduce evidence: for example, for instance, such as, to show this.
To conclude: finally, in conclusion, to sum up, as you can see.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your linked-up argument to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the linking words make your reasoning clearer, or whether any feel forced.
Ask the tutor to suggest one more linking word that would help my flow.

activities.title: Design a visual and a slogan
activities.label: Activity 7: Design a visual and a slogan
activities.intro: Some of your audience will meet your message through a visual rather than a talk. Design one now: a poster, a simple chart, or a diagram, with a short slogan to carry your message quickly.
steps: Decide the clearest visual for your evidence: a bar chart for numbers, a diagram for how something works, or a poster for awareness.
Sketch it. Keep it simple and easy to read from a distance.
Write a slogan: a short, memorable phrase that captures your key message.
Test your slogan: is it short, clear, and does it stick in the mind?

boxes.title: Model slogans
lines: Water: Every drop counts — do not waste water.
Road safety: Slow down outside our school — keep students safe.
Plastic: Say no to thin bags — bring your own.
Notice each one is short, clear, and gives a reason or a feeling.

A visual is not decoration; it should make one idea easier to grasp. If a passer-by cannot understand your poster in a few seconds, it is trying to say too much. Cut words until only your key message and your strongest piece of evidence remain. A single clear number, a simple drawing, and a short slogan will beat a crowded page every time.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your visual and read your slogan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the visual shows your evidence clearly and whether the slogan is memorable.
Ask the tutor for one way to make my slogan shorter or stronger.

activities.title: Match your language to your audience
activities.label: Activity 8: Match your language to your audience
activities.intro: Check that your register — your level of formality — fits your audience. The same message should sound different for young children, for family, and for officials.
steps: Write your key message in a friendly register, as if speaking to a younger child or your family.
Write the same message in a formal register, as if writing to the town council or head teacher.
Decide which register fits the audience you chose in Activity 1.
Adjust your presentation so its language matches that audience throughout.

boxes.title: Yasmin's example: one message, two registers
lines: Message: girls who leave school early lose chances they cannot easily get back.
Friendly (for younger students): staying in school opens doors that are hard to open later.
Formal (for a community meeting): early school-leaving among girls reduces their future opportunities, and I ask you to consider how we might support them to stay.
Same message, matched to each audience.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two versions — friendly and formal — to your AI tutor.
Ask it which register best fits my real audience, and why.
Ask the tutor to check that my presentation keeps that register from start to finish.

activities.title: Rehearse your full presentation with your AI tutor
activities.label: Activity 9: Rehearse your full presentation with your AI tutor
activities.intro: This is the most important activity in the unit. Before you present to real people, rehearse the whole thing out loud with your AI tutor acting as your audience. Rehearsing silently in your head is not the same; speaking out loud is what builds confidence.
steps: Present your whole talk out loud to your AI tutor, from introduction to conclusion.
Ask the tutor for feedback using three fair rules: start positive, more positives than negatives, and about the work.
Fix the one weakest part it points out.
Present the whole talk again. Notice how much clearer and calmer you feel the second time.

boxes.title: Rehearsal tips
lines: Speak slowly and clearly, and pause after your key message.
Use a few bullet-point notes, not a full script you read word for word.
Rehearse as many times as you like — your AI tutor never gets tired.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your full talk to your AI tutor and ask for honest feedback on clarity and pace.
Ask it to predict two questions a real audience might ask, and help me prepare answers.
Ask the tutor: what is the single most important thing to improve before my teacher session?

activities.title: Deliver in your teacher session and listen actively
activities.label: Activity 10: Deliver in your teacher session and listen actively
activities.intro:
Now for the real thing. You have rehearsed; you are ready. Deliver your presentation in your teacher session, and when it is someone else's turn, practise active listening.

It is completely normal to feel nervous before you present, even after rehearsing. Nerves are a sign that you care, not a sign that you are unprepared. Take a slow breath, remember that you know your topic better than anyone in the room, and keep your key message in your mind. Because you practised out loud with your AI tutor, your voice already knows the way.
steps: Deliver your presentation to your teacher and the other learners. Speak slowly, and remember your key message.
When others present, listen actively: nod, make eye contact, and use signals like 'I see'.
Give one classmate helpful feedback using the three fair rules.
Note down any questions your own audience asked, so you can reflect on them.

boxes.title: Share it at home too
lines: Present your Challenge to a family member or neighbour, in a register that suits them.
Ask them what they think should be done about your topic.
Bring their response, and any questions they asked, to your next teacher session.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor how your real presentation went and what questions people asked.
Ask it to help me understand what those questions show about the clearest and weakest parts of my talk.
Ask the tutor to help me plan one improvement for the next time I present.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'communication' mean?
practice.answer: Communication means transferring information from one person to another, by speaking or writing, so that the other person truly understands. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Communication has two halves: expressing your own ideas and ______ to others.
practice.answer: Listening.

practice.prompt: Before you plan any piece, you should know two things: your purpose and your ______.
practice.answer: Audience.

practice.prompt: Name the three main parts of a well-structured presentation.
practice.answer: Introduction, body (or middle), and conclusion.

practice.prompt: True or false: a good conclusion is the perfect place to add an exciting new fact.
practice.answer: False. A conclusion only sums up what you already said; it should not add new ideas.

practice.prompt: An argument is made of three parts: a claim, reasons, and ______.
practice.answer: Evidence.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a linking word? (a) elephant (b) because (c) quickly (d) blue.
practice.answer: (b) because.

practice.prompt: Give one linking word or phrase you could use to introduce a piece of evidence.
practice.answer: Any one of: for example, for instance, such as, to show this.

practice.prompt: When you present out loud, should you speak quickly to save time, or slowly and clearly?
practice.answer: Slowly and clearly.

practice.prompt: What is a slogan, and why are short sentences useful in one?
practice.answer: A slogan is a short, memorable phrase that raises awareness. Short sentences are used because they are easy to remember.

practice.prompt: The word ______ means the level of formality in your language, chosen to suit your audience.
practice.answer: Register.

practice.prompt: Active listening means attentively trying to ______ someone, not just hearing their words.
practice.answer: Understand (attentively trying to understand the person).

practice.prompt: Give one example of non-verbal feedback that shows you are listening.
practice.answer: Any one of: nodding, leaning forward, making eye contact.

practice.prompt: When you give feedback on someone's work, name one of the three fair rules.
practice.answer: Any one of: start with a positive; give more positives than negatives; talk about the work, not the person.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why you should reference the sources of your evidence when you communicate.
practice.answer: Any one of: it is honest and avoids copying; it lets the audience check your facts; it makes your work more trustworthy.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each communication word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Audience
options: A. Attentively trying to understand what someone says, not just hearing the words.
B. A claim supported by reasons and evidence.
C. The people you are communicating with.
D. The part of a piece that sums up the points and adds nothing new.
E. Choosing your level of language to suit your audience and purpose.
F. A short, memorable phrase used to raise awareness of an issue.
practice.answer: C — The people you are communicating with.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Register
practice.answer: E — Choosing your level of language to suit your audience and purpose.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Argument
practice.answer: B — A claim supported by reasons and evidence.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Slogan
practice.answer: F — A short, memorable phrase used to raise awareness of an issue.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Active listening
practice.answer: A — Attentively trying to understand what someone says, not just hearing the words.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Conclusion
practice.answer: D — The part of a piece that sums up the points and adds nothing new.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Nadia is presenting about hand-washing to a class of six-year-olds. Should her register be formal and technical, or simple and friendly? Why?
practice.answer: Simple and friendly. Six-year-olds would not follow formal, technical language, so a warm, simple register suits them best.

practice.prompt: Omar ends his talk by suddenly adding a brand-new statistic he never mentioned before. Which rule of a good conclusion has he broken?
practice.answer: He added a new idea in the conclusion. A conclusion should only sum up points already made, not introduce new facts.

practice.prompt: Zara tells her audience 'our streets are dirty' but gives nothing else. What one thing should she add so the audience believes her?
practice.answer: Evidence. She should add a fact, number or example (and its source) so the audience has a reason to believe her.

practice.prompt: During Arjun's talk, Leila nods and quietly says 'I see.' What is she doing, and why does it help?
practice.answer: She is listening actively and giving verbal and non-verbal feedback. It helps because it shows Arjun she is paying attention and understanding him.

practice.prompt: Karim needs a poster slogan about saving water. Which is better, and why: 'Every drop counts — do not waste water', or 'Water is something we should all be careful about using in our daily lives'?
practice.answer: 'Every drop counts — do not waste water' is better because it is short, clear and memorable, which is exactly what a slogan needs.

vocabulary.meaning: Transferring information from one person to another, usually by speaking or writing.
The reason you are communicating: to inform, to persuade, or to raise awareness.
The people you are communicating with.
The single most important idea you want your audience to remember.
How a piece is organised so the audience can follow it.
The opening that says what a piece is about and states its message.
The middle of a piece, where the main points and evidence are given.
The ending that sums up the points made, without adding anything new.
A group of sentences presenting one main idea and its details.
A claim supported by reasons and evidence.
What you want your audience to accept as true.
Why a claim is true.
A fact, number or example that supports a claim.
Where a piece of information or evidence came from.
A note saying exactly where information came from.
All the sources used, gathered together at the end of a piece.
Explaining why, by connecting your points with reasons.
Linking words that connect ideas, such as because and for example.
A short, memorable phrase used to raise awareness of an issue.
The level of formality in language, chosen to suit the audience.
A particular point of view on an issue.
Someone who has an interest in an issue and may be affected by it.
Attentively trying to understand a speaker, not just hearing their words.
Spoken signals that show you are listening, such as 'I see' or 'I understand'.
Signals without words, such as nodding, leaning forward, or eye contact.
Helpful information given to someone about their work.
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
When a source or speaker leans unfairly to one side.

mistakes: Starting to plan before you know your purpose and audience.
Having no clear key message, so the audience misses your point.
Making a claim with no reason or evidence behind it.
Sneaking a brand-new idea into the conclusion.
Speaking too fast and never pausing.
Using a register that does not fit the audience.
Forgetting to reference where your evidence came from.
Only speaking, and never really listening to others.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'communication' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Communication means transferring information from one person to another, by speaking or writing, so that the other person truly understands. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: Communication has two halves: expressing your own ideas and ______ to others.
Before you plan any piece, you should know two things: your purpose and your ______.
Name the three main parts of a well-structured presentation.
True or false: a good conclusion is the perfect place to add an exciting new fact.
questions.modelAnswer: False. A conclusion only sums up what you already said; it should not add new ideas.

questions.prompt: An argument is made of three parts: a claim, reasons, and ______.
Which of these is a linking word? (a) elephant (b) because (c) quickly (d) blue.
Give one linking word or phrase you could use to introduce a piece of evidence.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: for example, for instance, such as, to show this.

questions.prompt: When you present out loud, should you speak quickly to save time, or slowly and clearly?
What is a slogan, and why are short sentences useful in one?
questions.modelAnswer: A slogan is a short, memorable phrase that raises awareness. Short sentences are used because they are easy to remember.

questions.prompt: The word ______ means the level of formality in your language, chosen to suit your audience.
Active listening means attentively trying to ______ someone, not just hearing their words.
questions.modelAnswer: Understand (attentively trying to understand the person).

selfAssessment.statement: I can plan a piece of communication for a clear purpose and audience.
I can say my key message in one clear sentence.
I can organise my ideas into an introduction, a body and a conclusion.
I can build a point as a claim with a reason and evidence.
I can reference the sources my evidence came from.
I can use linking words to give reasons and connect my ideas.
I can present clearly out loud, speaking slowly and clearly.
I can present my ideas visually, for example with a poster or slogan.
I can choose suitable language and register for my audience.
I can listen actively and give helpful, kind feedback.
